title: Kings at War, Faith Under Pressure
overview: A heavenly messenger traces centuries of power struggles, from Persia through Alexander's successors, down to a Syrian king who tries to stamp out Jewish faith in Jerusalem.

parts.label: Persia to Alexander (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The messenger from chapter 10 says that in the first year of Darius the Mede he stood by to strengthen 'him'; some read 'him' as Darius, others as the angel Michael named just before in 10:21 (v. 1). He then traces Persian kings to a very rich fourth, usually taken as Xerxes, who invaded Greece, and a 'mighty king,' widely taken as Alexander the Great, whose empire split apart instead of passing to his family (vv. 2-4).

parts.label: Wars of north and south (vv. 5-20)
parts.note: The 'king of the south' stands for the Greek dynasty ruling Egypt and the 'king of the north' for the one ruling Syria, with Judea caught between them (v. 16, where translations call it the glorious or the beautiful land). Readers commonly match the details to known events, such as an Egyptian princess sent to marry the Syrian king and later murdered (v. 6), and the Syrian king Antiochus III taking Judea, losing to Rome (v. 18) and dying soon after (v. 19).

parts.label: A contemptible king rises (vv. 21-30)
parts.note: Interpreters across traditions identify this 'contemptible person' as Antiochus IV, who took the Syrian throne by scheming (v. 21) and invaded Egypt (vv. 25-28). When ships from the west forced him back (v. 30, where some translations keep the old name Kittim, usually taken as Roman ships or envoys), he turned his anger on 'the holy covenant,' meaning the Jewish faith and people, and favored those who abandoned it.

parts.label: Temple defiled, faithful suffer (vv. 31-35)
parts.note: His forces defiled the temple, stopped its regular daily offerings and set up a desolating 'abomination,' a word for a detested object of false worship, usually understood as a pagan altar built over the temple altar around 167 BC (v. 31). The 'wise' who resisted were killed, burned, captured or robbed, and the text presents this as refining them (vv. 33-35), while the 'little help' (v. 34) is often taken to be the Jewish revolt led by the Maccabee family.

parts.label: The king who exalts himself (vv. 36-39)
parts.note: This king puts himself above every god and honors a 'god of fortresses' (v. 38), often thought to be Zeus, whose worship Antiochus brought into the temple; verse 37's mention of what women desire is unclear and worded differently across translations, with guesses ranging from a god popular with women to ordinary human affection. Many read these lines as still about Antiochus, while some Christians, noting echoes in 2 Thessalonians 2:4, see them as also or mainly describing a final enemy at the end of history.

parts.label: A final campaign and end (vv. 40-45)
parts.note: The king sweeps through Judea and Egypt, pitches his royal tents by 'the holy mountain,' usually taken as Jerusalem, and then comes to his end with no one to help him (v. 45), though the text does not say where he dies. Antiochus IV in fact died in Persia around 164 BC, so many scholars who date the chapter to his lifetime see a real prediction written shortly before his death that did not unfold as described, while others read a recap of his earlier wars or a picture of a ruler still to come.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this detailed history was foretold in Daniel's own day, as many conservative Protestants hold, or written during Antiochus's persecution in the 160s BC, as most modern scholars (including many Catholic and mainline Protestant ones) hold, and on whether verses 36 to 45 still describe Antiochus or also point to a final enemy at the end of history.
think: What do you think makes some people hold to their convictions under heavy pressure while others quietly let them go?
